[RFCS.3.4] **Atom injection classification (the codec rule).** On
replay each atom is exactly one of three classes, and the class fixes
what a reader may do with it. **Which atom is in which class is the
`Stream-class` column of [RFCS.3.1]**, its single normative home; this
clause states what each class obliges a reader to do.

- **inject** — recorded external inputs; the replayer delivers them to
  the engine as recorded ([LFST.9.2]).
- **compare** — engine-produced annotations and outbound effects; the
  replayer re-derives them and byte-compares to the record ([LFST.9.3])
  and **must not** deliver them to the engine.
- **structural / ignore** — framing, schema and seek atoms with no
  replay-input meaning.

**This clause binds replay** ([LFST.9.6]), which runs the engine and compares
what it produces, so for it the three classes are three different obligations.
There is one operation for the rule to bind, and no mode within it reads an
atom differently.

A re-deriving reader's inject path **MUST refuse** any atom outside the
inject class — delivering a `CallIssued` (or `RuleFireAnnotation`) to the engine as an input would
corrupt determinism, and skipping an inject-class atom would drop a real
input. This makes the load-bearing invariant — **a `call` is never a
replay input** — a rule the codec enforces rather than a convention (it
is the same invariant the stream-transducer unification carries verbatim
across live and recorded transports). The classification also fixes
skip-safety for an *unknown* field number. A future atom is safely skippable
([RFCS.2.3]) only if **both** hold: it is compare or structural, **and it
carries no positional precondition** — no claim about the state the stream
begins in, or about where in the stream it sits. A new inject-class atom is
not additive — an older reader cannot skip it without losing an input it was
handed — so it lands with a minor release ([LDET.1.10]).

**The second condition is needed because the first alone is false.** A structural atom announcing that a stream *continues from*
another is skippable by class and catastrophic to skip in fact: a reader that
ignores it replays a mid-run segment as though it began at genesis, with an
empty working memory it never had. That is silently wrong output rather than a
refusal, and no property of the atom's class predicts it — the hazard is
positional. Such an atom is allocated in the reject-don't-skip band
([RFCS.16.2]) even though its class would otherwise permit skipping.
